text: We have this mental metaphor that we talk a lot about, getting to the next hill.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: At the beginning of the podcast, Noah explains Slack's approach to product innovation and avoiding incremental thinking. He describes how product teams can get trapped in constant small improvements without seeing bigger opportunities. The metaphor of "getting to the next hill" refers to moving beyond immediate tasks to see the broader landscape of possibilities that exists beyond current projects.
text_ko: 우리가 자주 하는 얘기 중에 마음속 은유(mental metaphor) 하나 있어요: 바로 '다음 언덕으로 가는 것(getting to the next hill)'이에요.
text_zh: 我们常提的一个心理比喻就是“翻过下一座山头”。
text_es: Hay una metáfora mental de la que hablamos mucho: llegar a la siguiente colina.
original_text: We have this mental metaphor that we talk a lot about, getting to the next hill. The actual wording is "Take bigger boulder bets." I think teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it where we've over time freighted new teams from scratch that incubated in a new area before the areas mature.

vocabulary.definition: A figure of speech that describes an object or action in a way that isn’t literally true, often used to illustrate a concept or idea.
vocabulary.businessContext: Metaphors are commonly used in business communication to simplify complex ideas and make them more relatable to stakeholders.
vocabulary.nuance: While effective for illustration, metaphors can sometimes obscure meaning if overused or poorly chosen.

text: I think the biggest probably lesson learned, frankly, is that we were really close with the Instagram folks early on. They were big developers on our platform. They used the Foursquare API before they were bought by Facebook.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: Lenny asks Noah whether Foursquare could have built a massive consumer business or if pivoting to B2B data was inevitable. Noah reflects on what went wrong with Foursquare's social strategy. He explains that they focused on location-based sharing (person + place) while Instagram succeeded with experience-based sharing (person + moment), which sometimes included location but wasn't dependent on it.
text_ko: 솔직히 제가 생각하기에 가장 큰 교훈은 초기에 인스타그램 쪽과 우리가 정말 가까웠다는 점이에요. 그들은 우리 플랫폼에서 중요한 개발자들이었고, 페이스북에 인수되기 전에 포스퀘어 API(Foursquare API)를 사용했어요.
text_zh: 老实说，我觉得最重要的一个教训，大概就是我们当年和 Instagram（Instagram）团队走得很近。他们当时是我们平台上很重要的开发者，在被 Facebook（Facebook）收购之前就一直在用 Foursquare 的 API（Foursquare API）。
text_es: Creo que, para ser sincero, la lección más importante fue que desde el principio teníamos muy buena relación con la gente de Instagram. Eran de los desarrolladores (developers) más importantes de nuestra plataforma y usaban la interfaz de programación (API) de Foursquare antes de que Facebook la comprara.
key_sentence: we were really close with the Instagram folks early on.
original_text: I think the biggest probably lesson learned, frankly, is that we were really close with the Instagram folks early on. They were big developers on our platform. They used the Foursquare API before they were bought by Facebook. I think in hindsight we were a little bit mistaken to believe that the idea that the atomic unit would be a person talking about a place that they're at and you have to have a physical place to tie it to versus a person sharing a moment or an experience that they're having in the world.

vocabulary.definition: A platform is a foundational technology or service that enables the development and deployment of applications, products, or services, often facilitating interactions between users and providers.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, platforms like social media networks or software ecosystems serve as critical infrastructures that support third-party developers and enhance user engagement.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a broader ecosystem of services and users, and is often associated with scalability and network effects.

vocabulary.definition: Developers are individuals or teams responsible for creating, building, and maintaining software applications or systems, often possessing specialized technical skills.
vocabulary.businessContext: In technology companies, developers play a crucial role in product development, innovation, and the implementation of new features that meet user needs.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can encompass a range of roles, from front-end to back-end developers, and is often associated with collaboration and problem-solving in tech environments.

text: I would say to folks in general, if you're joining company and the CEO does the role that is your functional area of expertise, it's probably the area where you'll learn the most because they're hopefully world class at it.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: Lenny asks Noah about working with strong product-minded founders like Dennis Crowley and Stewart Butterfield. Noah shares advice for product managers joining companies where the CEO is deeply involved in product decisions. He explains the trade-off between learning opportunities and potential frustration when working under a product-focused founder who may limit your decision-making authority.
text_ko: 일반적으로 사람들에게 이렇게 말하고 싶어요. 회사에 합류할 때 최고경영자(CEO)가 당신의 전문 분야(functional area)를 직접 맡고 있다면, 그게 아마 당신이 가장 많이 배우는 분야일 거예요. 그분이 그 일을 세계적 수준으로 잘할 가능성이 크기 때문이에요.
text_zh: 我一般会跟大家说，如果你要加入的公司里，首席执行官（CEO）亲自负责的恰好是你擅长的那个职能领域，那通常就是你能学到最多的地方，因为你可以指望他们在这方面是世界级的。
text_es: Diría, en general, que si entras a una empresa y el CEO desempeña el rol de tu área funcional (functional area), probablemente sea el área donde más vas a aprender, porque con suerte será de primer nivel (world-class) en eso.
key_sentence: Joining a company with a CEO in your functional area of expertise offers less agency.
original_text: I would say to folks in general, if you're joining company and the CEO does the role that is your functional area of expertise, it's probably the area where you'll learn the most because they're hopefully world class at it. But also, one will you'll be the most frustrated at times because you're going to feel like you have less agency.

vocabulary.definition: A specific division or department within an organization that focuses on a particular set of tasks or responsibilities.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, functional areas such as marketing, finance, and human resources are essential for the overall operation and strategic direction of the company.
vocabulary.nuance: While often used to describe distinct departments, 'functional area' can also imply a specialization within a broader role, highlighting the importance of expertise in that domain.

vocabulary.definition: A high level of knowledge or skill in a particular area or field, often acquired through experience and education.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, having expertise is crucial for making informed decisions, driving innovation, and maintaining competitive advantage.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a connotation of authority and trustworthiness, suggesting that the individual is not only knowledgeable but also respected in their field.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to the highest standard of quality or performance, often recognized internationally as exemplary.
vocabulary.businessContext: Companies strive to achieve world-class status to enhance their reputation, attract top talent, and gain a competitive edge in the global market.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase implies not just excellence, but also a benchmark against which others are measured, making it a powerful descriptor in marketing and branding.

text: I think what we would wind up doing with Stewart at Slack, for example, is we would get the entire development team, engineers design product, user research and Stewart together in a room and we almost do a bug bash together.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: Noah explains how to successfully involve product-minded founders in the final stages of product development. He describes Slack's collaborative approach where the entire team, including founder Stewart Butterfield, would gather to review and refine products before launch. A "bug bash" is a collaborative session where team members test software together to find and fix issues.
text_ko: 예를 들어 Slack의 스튜어트와 함께라면 개발팀 전체—엔지니어, 디자이너, 제품팀, 사용자 리서치(user research) 담당자와 스튜어트를 한 방에 모아놓고 사실상 함께 버그 바시(bug bash)를 하곤 해요.
text_zh: 我觉得像跟 Slack 那边的 Stewart 合作时，我们会把整个开发团队、工程师、设计、产品、用户研究这些人连同 Stewart 一起叫到一个房间，然后大家一起集中找 bug（bug bash）。
text_es: Creo que, por ejemplo, con Stewart en Slack lo que acabaríamos haciendo sería reunir en una sala a todo el equipo de desarrollo —ingeniería, diseño, producto e investigación de usuarios— y prácticamente hacer entre todos una revisión masiva de errores (bug bash).
key_sentence: We wind up doing a bug bash together to clean up the mess collaboratively.
original_text: I think what we would wind up doing with Stewart at Slack, for example, is we would get the entire development team, engineers design product, user research and Stewart together in a room and we almost do a bug bash together. The idea was like, "We're doing it all together. We're trying to make the best product possible, making great softwares really messy and we're all trying to clean up the mess together."

vocabulary.definition: A group of professionals, typically including software engineers, designers, and product managers, responsible for creating and improving products or services.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech companies, the development team plays a crucial role in the product lifecycle, from initial concept through to deployment and maintenance.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can vary in composition and focus depending on the organization, with some teams emphasizing agile methodologies or cross-functional collaboration.

text: What we started doing with these complaints storms and idea was really simple, which is we'd get a team together often Stewart myself would also join and we'd actually start off with other products first in adjacent spaces and we'd say, "Okay.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: Lenny asks Noah about Slack's "Complaint-Storms" process. Noah explains this method for helping teams look at their product with fresh eyes and build empathy for new users. The process involves teams critically examining customer journeys in competing products first, then applying the same critical lens to their own product to identify pain points and areas for improvement.
text_ko: 우리가 이런 불만 폭주(complaints storms)와 아이디어로 시작할 때 한 일은 정말 단순했어요. 팀을 모으고 스튜어트도 자주, 저도 함께 참여했는데, 실제로 먼저 인접 분야(adjacent spaces)의 다른 제품들부터 살펴보면서 "좋아요."라고 말하곤 했어요.
text_zh: 我们开始用这些“投诉风暴”(complaints storms)和想法着手做的事其实很简单：把团队凑在一起，Stewart 常来，我也会参加。我们通常先从相近领域的其他产品下手，然后会说，“好。”
text_es: Lo que empezamos a hacer con estas oleadas de quejas (complaints storms) fue muy sencillo: reuníamos a un equipo —a menudo Stewart se unía y yo también— y, en realidad, empezábamos por otros productos en áreas afines y decíamos: "vale".
key_sentence: we'd actually start off with other products first in adjacent spaces
original_text: What we started doing with these complaints storms and idea was really simple, which is we'd get a team together often Stewart myself would also join and we'd actually start off with other products first in adjacent spaces and we'd say, "Okay. As a group we're going to go through the customer journey from the moment you land on the website through, let's say it's a workplace product, getting your first account going, getting the first couple of users on board, getting to the point of value."

vocabulary.definition: Next to or adjoining something else; having a common boundary.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'adjacent' often refers to markets or sectors that are closely related or similar to a company's current operations, allowing for potential expansion or synergy.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'adjacent' implies proximity, it often carries a connotation of strategic relevance, suggesting that the adjacent area is worth exploring for growth opportunities.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals working collaboratively towards a common goal.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, a 'team' is essential for leveraging diverse skills and perspectives, driving projects forward, and fostering innovation through collaboration.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'team' often implies a sense of unity and shared responsibility, but it can also carry implications of hierarchy or role differentiation depending on the context.

text: I think teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it. Take bigger boulder bets. Get to the next hill to see what the horizon wants around you.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: Lenny asks how Slack enables innovation and zero-to-one bets despite being a large company. Noah explains Slack's strategic philosophy using a mountain climbing metaphor. He describes how teams can get trapped focusing on immediate incremental improvements ("crawling up that hill") without seeing the much larger opportunities that exist beyond their current scope.
text_ko: 팀들은 종종 그 언덕을 기어 오르다 길을 잃고, 그 뒤에 거대한 멋진 산맥이 있다는 걸 깨닫지 못해요. 더 과감한 베팅(boulder bets)을 해보세요. 다음 언덕까지 올라가서 지평선을 보면 주변에 어떤 기회들이 있는지 알 수 있어요.
text_zh: 很多团队常常在眼前这座小坡上耗着，没看到背后有一大片更宏大、更漂亮的天地。要敢下更大的赌注（boulder bets）。爬到下一个山头，看看地平线周围有哪些机会。
text_es: Creo que los equipos a menudo se pierden arrastrándose cuesta arriba por esa colina, sin darse cuenta de que detrás hay una cordillera enorme e increíblemente hermosa. Hagan apuestas más grandes (boulder bets). Suban a la siguiente colina para ver qué hay en el horizonte.
key_sentence: Take bigger boulder bets to see what the horizon wants around you.
original_text: I think teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it. Take bigger boulder bets. Get to the next hill to see what the horizon wants around you. That's how we think about it strategically.

vocabulary.definition: The line at which the earth's surface and the sky appear to meet; metaphorically, it refers to the limit of one's knowledge, experience, or interest.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'horizon' is often used to describe future opportunities or challenges that an organization may face, encouraging teams to look beyond immediate concerns.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a sense of optimism and potential, suggesting that there are greater opportunities ahead if one looks beyond current limitations.

vocabulary.definition: A term used to describe significant, high-stakes investments or decisions that have the potential for substantial returns or consequences.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and business strategy, 'boulder bets' refer to bold moves that can define a company's future direction and success, often involving considerable risk.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase suggests a willingness to take calculated risks for potentially transformative outcomes, and it is typically used in discussions about innovation and growth strategies.

text: I think when we have those teams, I think it's important to just give them space to run, to give them ... get a gel free card for maybe the normal process of, "Okay.
speaker: Noah Weiss
context: Noah continues explaining how Slack structures innovation teams to work on new product areas like AI. He emphasizes giving these teams freedom from normal corporate processes and focusing on learning velocity rather than traditional planning cycles. The goal is rapid prototyping and user learning that eventually leads to breakthrough products that exceed customer expectations.
text_ko: 그런 팀이 생기면 그냥 마음껏 달려보라고 여지를 주는 게 중요하다고 생각해요. 평소 프로세스에서 잠깐 벗어날 수 있는 일종의 면죄부(get-out-of-jail-free card)를 줘야 해요.
text_zh: 我觉得有那样的团队时，重要的是放手给他们空间去运作，甚至在某些常规流程上给他们一张免死金牌(get-out-of-jail-free card)。
text_es: Creo que cuando tenemos esos equipos, es importante darles espacio para que actúen, darles una especie de carta blanca para saltarse el proceso normal de “vale…”.
key_sentence: it's important to just give them space to run, to give them ... get a gel free card for maybe the normal process
original_text: I think when we have those teams, I think it's important to just give them space to run, to give them ... get a gel free card for maybe the normal process of, "Okay. Our planning quarterly reviews" and make it feel something that is the pace of learning is what matters. How fast are you prototyping, how fast are you learning from users and then getting to do that publicly and pilot and then get something to launch that's amazing, blows people away.
